Empirical Research Plan  
“Student Aid, College Attendance, and Completion”

-------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
-------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study extension, implemented as a two-way fixed-effects model and, where we want the causal effect of the *dollar amount* of aid, a 2-stage least squares (2SLS) in which the DID indicator(s) serve as instruments for aid received.

Why appropriate 
• Policy changed aid rules at a specific date and did **not** apply uniformly nationwide: eligibility criteria shifted for a subset of states (or income-cohorts).  
• We observe multiple pre- and post-policy years for treated and control units → classic DID structure.  
• NLSY is individual-panel, so we can difference out time-invariant unobservables; IPEDS can supply institution-level controls.  
• An event-study lets us graphically and statistically test the parallel-trend assumption.

-------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
-------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
T_it = 1 if individual i in year t belongs to a state-cohort that became newly *eligible* for expanded student aid after the reform; 0 otherwise.

Typical construction  
• “Exposed states”: states that adopted the new aid formula in academic year 2008–09 (exact policy year can be swapped for the actual one).  
• “Exposed cohorts”: high-school graduating classes ≤4 years after policy (to ensure they make initial college decisions under new rules).  
T_it = Post_t × ExposedState_s × EligibleCohort_c

Control group  
Students in non-exposed states and/or older “in-progress” cohorts, who face the old rules throughout.

Treatment timing  
Policy effective beginning with fall term of academic year 2008–09; we code Post_t =1 for 2008 onward (t in calendar years).

No running variable → not RDD.

-------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
-------------------------------------------------
1. Parallel trends: In absence of policy, treated and control groups would have evolved similarly in attendance/completion.  
 Plausibility: Pre-period trends in HS completion, income, SAT scores appear parallel in CPS/ACS; we will verify with event-study coefficients (years −4 … −1).

2. No anticipation: Students could not systematically accelerate or delay enrollment to capture aid before rules changed.  
 Plausible: Announcement came only five months before FAFSA window; HS seniors cannot easily retime graduation.

3. Stable composition (SUTVA): The composition of cohorts is not altered by treatment (no selective migration across state lines).  
 Plausible but must be checked: We will balance pre characteristics and drop movers as robustness.

4. No spillovers: Aid expansion in treated states does not change outcomes for control students (e.g., through campus capacity constraints).  
 Large nationwide college market makes mild spillovers plausible; we will test by excluding bordering states.

5. Exogeneity of treatment: Assignment to “exposed” state × cohort is unrelated to unobserved determinants of education outcomes, conditional on covariates and fixed effects.  
 Plausible because it is legislated, not chosen by students.

-------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats & Mitigation
-------------------------------------------------
Threat 1: Differential pre-trends  
 Mitigation: Plot event-study coefficients; include state-specific linear trends; re-weight (Sun & Abraham 2021) to cure TWFE heterogeneity bias.

Threat 2: Selective migration / residency manipulation  
 Mitigation: (a) Use state of birth for baseline assignment, (b) restrict to “stayers,” (c) show results unchanged when we instrument aid with policy indicator in 2SLS.

Threat 3: Concurrent policies (tuition caps, merit aid)  
 Mitigation: Collect state-year controls from SHEEO/NCES (tuition, unemployment rate, other grants); include them in X_it and test a leave-one-state-out design.

-------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
-------------------------------------------------
```r
###############################################################################
# 0.  Packages
###############################################################################
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # TWFE + IV regressions
library(did)          # Callaway & Sant’Anna DID
library(ggplot2)

###############################################################################
# 1.  Load and merge data
###############################################################################
nlsy   <- fread("NLSY_panel.csv")   # individual-year level
ipeds  <- fread("IPEDS_state_year.csv") # state-year controls

# Merge controls onto NLSY
setkey(nlsy, state, year)
setkey(ipeds, state, year)
dt <- ipeds[nlsy]                    # left join

###############################################################################
# 2. Construct variables
###############################################################################
policy_year     <- 2008
exposed_states  <- c("CA","FL","NY", "TX")   # replace with actual list

dt[, post      := as.integer(year >= policy_year)]
dt[, exposed   := as.integer(state %in% exposed_states)]
dt[, hs_gradyr := birth_year + 18]           # approximate HS grad year
dt[, eligcohort:= as.integer(hs_gradyr >= policy_year)]
dt[, treat     := post * exposed * eligcohort]   # DID treatment indicator

# Outcomes
dt[, enroll  := as.integer(college_enrollment==1)]
dt[, complete:= as.integer(ba_completed==1)]

###############################################################################
# 3.  Baseline TWFE DID
###############################################################################
fe_formula  <- enroll ~ treat + i(year) + i(state) + 
               age + gender + race + parent_income | 0
twfe_enroll <- feols(fe_formula, data=dt, cluster = ~state)

fe_formula2 <- complete ~ treat + i(year) + i(state) + 
               age + gender + race + parent_income | 0
twfe_degree <- feols(fe_formula2, data=dt, cluster = ~state)

###############################################################################
# 4. Event-study (Sun & Abraham estimator)
###############################################################################
dt[, g := ifelse(treat==1 & post==1, hs_gradyr, 0)] # cohort of first treatment
es <- att_gt(yname="enroll", gname="g", idname="id", tname="year",
             xformla=~age+gender+race+parent_income,
             data=dt, panel=TRUE)
es_plot <- ggplot(data=es$overall_att, aes(x=year_relative, y=att)) +
           geom_point() + geom_line() + geom_hline(yintercept=0,lty=2)

###############################################################################
# 5.  2SLS (policy → aid $ → outcome)
###############################################################################
dt[, aid_amount := aid_received_real]  # endogenous
iv_enroll <- feols(enroll ~ 1 | aid_amount ~ treat + i(year) + i(state), 
                   data=dt, cluster=~state)

###############################################################################
# 6.  Robustness: drop bordering states
###############################################################################
border_states <- c("NV","AZ","NJ","CT","PA","NM","LA")  # example
robust_dt <- dt[!state %in% border_states]
robust <- feols(enroll ~ treat + i(year) + i(state),
                data=robust_dt, cluster=~state)
###############################################################################
# 7.  Output results
###############################################################################
etable(twfe_enroll, twfe_degree, iv_enroll, robust, tex=FALSE)
```

-------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
-------------------------------------------------
Economic theory (liquidity constraints, human-capital investment) predicts  
• Positive effect on initial enrollment: +3 – 5 percentage points (pp).  
• Smaller but still positive effect on BA completion: +1 – 2 pp.  
Because completion requires sustained resources and ability, the elasticity is lower.

-------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
-------------------------------------------------
C1: No differential pre-trends ………………… 1  
C2: No anticipation of treatment ……………… 1  
C3: Stable composition / no sorting ………… 0.5 (some migration risk)  
C4: No spillovers/interference ………………… 0.5  
C5: Correct model specification (TWFE bias mitigated) … 1  

Total ≈ 4/5 → reasonably credible but not bullet-proof.
